title: Infra Team Wiki: GPU Fleet Capacity, Cloud Accounts & Networking, IaC Modules, CI/CD and Runbooks (Ops Guide)
author: Avery Chen
body:
Overview

This page is the consolidated operations guide for the infrastructure engineering team covering: GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud account and networking conventions, Terraform / IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and critical runbooks used during day-to-day operations and incidents. It is intended for engineers oncall for infra, platform, and serving-runtime and for engineers onboarding to GPU fleet ops.

Scope and goals
- Provide a single, practical reference for the infra team with actionable thresholds, ownership, commands, and links to runbooks.
- Standardize IaC module usage and CI/CD patterns to reduce configuration drift.
- Document capacity planning cadence and emergency provisioning flow for unexpected demand.

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-ops (pager duty: infra-oncall)
- Steward: Avery Chen (infra engineering) - avery.chen@redwood.example.com
- Reviewers: Kai Morgan (cloud accounts), Priya Desai (networking), Liam O'Connor (ci/cd)
- Service owners referenced in this doc are responsible for keeping module versions and runbooks updated.

High-level architecture references
- GPU fleet control plane: infra-gpu-controller (k8s operator)
- Capacity autoscaler: fleet-autoscaler-service (internal microservice)
- IaC modules: terraform-modules/aws-account, terraform-modules/networking, terraform-modules/gpu-nodegroup
- CI/CD: infra-pipelines (GitHub Actions), module-publish (internal registry)

GPU Fleet & Capacity

1) Capacity planning cadence
- Weekly: short-run utilization report (1h/24h/7d percentiles) published every Monday by 09:00 PT. Owner: capacity-team.
- Monthly: capacity review meeting on first Monday of the month. Action items: resize reserved pools, adjust burst policies, bump nodegroup sizes.
- Quarterly: forecast (Q) based on sales commits and Dedicated reservations.

2) SLOs and thresholds
- Target utilization (steady-state): 55% - 70% across dedicated pools.
- Alert thresholds:
  - P1 Alert: available GPU nodes < 8% of pool capacity (notify oncall immediately)
  - P2 Alert: pending pods > 5% of queue for > 10 minutes
  - Cost alert: sustained unit-cost per token increases by > 20% week-over-week

3) Emergency provisioning flow (short version)
1. Triage: confirm increased demand using Grafana dashboard (dashboards/fleet/usage).
2. If immediate capacity needed: run terraform apply against the gpu-nodegroup module with the emergency variable set (see IaC section).
3. Notify stakeholders in #infra-ops and open a capacity incident in PagerDuty.
4. After remediation, create a post-incident action to right-size reserved capacity.

4) Operational checks and commands
- Check node health (k8s): kubectl get nodes -l node-pool=gpu -o wide
- Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- Fleet autoscaler status: curl -sS http://fleet-autoscaler.internal/health | jq .

Cloud Accounts and Networking

Principles
- Keep a 1:1 mapping between logical account (prod/staging/dedicated) and tenant AWS account when possible.
- Networking must be explicit: no implicit cross-account peering without documented approval.
- Least privilege for service IAM roles; prefer assume-role patterns between accounts.

Account naming and tagging standard
- Account name format: redwood-{environment}-{purpose}-{region} (e.g., redwood-prod-dedicated-us-west-2)
- Required tags on all resources: owner, cost_center, environment, team, service

VPC & connectivity patterns
- Shared VPC for infra services (centralized NAT, logging, and transit gateway).
- Per-account VPC for customer-dedicated workloads with Transit Gateway attachments.
- Allowed egress: only to approved vendor endpoints. For air-gapped/private deployments use private endpoints and VPC endpoints for S3/KMS.

Network security controls
- NACLs and security groups follow deny-by-default principle.
- Central firewall (managed by network-team) enforces cross-account flows.

Terraform / IaC modules

Module policy
- All changes to terraform-modules/* must be merged with a module change PR and accompany an example in the module's examples/ directory.
- Module versioning via semver; releases published to internal module registry.

Common modules and usage examples
- terraform-modules/aws-account (creates IAM roles, account-level config)
- terraform-modules/networking (VPC, subnets, route tables, transit gateway attachments)
- terraform-modules/gpu-nodegroup (autoscaling group/nodegroup for GPU instances)

Example: gpu-nodegroup usage

module "gpu_nodegroup" {
  source = "internal/terraform-modules/gpu-nodegroup"
  version = "1.3.2"

  cluster_name = "prod-gpu-cluster"
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  min_size = 2
  desired_size = 10
  max_size = 50
  labels = { workload = "inference" }
  emergency_scale_multiplier = 2
}

Notes: emergency_scale_multiplier is used by the emergency provisioning flow to quickly double desired capacity for bursts; use only with approval.

IaC CI/CD patterns
- Branch protection: all module repos require two approvers and a successful plan check.
- Plan check: PRs must run terraform plan in a sandbox account and upload plan artifacts.
- Auto-apply rules: Only approved branches (release/*) may auto-apply via the infra-pipelines runner.

CI/CD and Build (Infra pipelines)

Pipeline components
- infra-pipelines (GitHub Actions) - runs lint, fmt, plan, test, publish module artifacts.
- module-publish - publishes module tarballs to the internal registry and tags docker images.
- cluster-deploy - gated workflow that runs manual approval before applying changes to prod accounts.

Standard pipeline steps for module repo
1. on: pull_request -> run: terraform fmt, tflint, terraform init, terraform validate, terraform plan (sandbox)
2. on: push tag -> run: acceptance tests, build artifacts, publish to registry, create release notes
3. scheduled: module-dependency-scan weekly for drift detection

Secrets and credentials
- Use HashiCorp Vault for long-lived credentials and short-lived AWS creds via IAM role/OIDC.
- CI runners fetch short-lived creds using role-assume with MFA for apply jobs.

Runbooks and Playbooks

Critical runbooks (short list)
- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook (primary) - steps for capacity alerts, emergency scaling, and rollback.
- network-transit-gw-incident - triage for Transit Gateway issues and cross-account routing failures.
- terraform-apply-failure - rollback and plan re-run checklist.

Example runbook excerpt: GPU capacity P1
1. PagerDuty fires: available GPU nodes < 8%
2. Oncall: acknowledge and escalate to capacity owner
3. Check cluster autoscaler metrics and pending pods: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
4. If autoscaler not kicking, manually increase nodegroup desired_size via terraform in the staging-account sandbox and run apply to prod (follow emergency approval process)
5. After scaling, validate scheduling (kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide) and cost signals.
6. Post-incident: create incident in Jira and schedule capacity review.

Postmortem and Documentation Rules
- Every P1 incident must have a postmortem within 72 hours with action owners and due dates.
- Update runbooks within 7 days of incident if the runbook steps were insufficient.

Operational tooling and dashboards
- Dashboards:
  - dashboards/fleet/usage (utilization, active jobs, queue lengths)
  - dashboards/cost/unit-cost (per-token unit cost; model-level breakdown)
  - dashboards/ci/module-pipeline (pipeline health and flaky tests)
- Tools:
  - infra-cli (internal tool) for account switch and apply helpers: infra-cli switch-account prod && infra-cli plan gpu-nodegroup
  - module-registry UI: https://modules.internal.redwood.example.com

Maintenance windows and change management
- Weekly maintenance window: Saturdays 02:00-06:00 PT for non-prod; Sundays 01:00-05:00 PT for prod (emergency-only changes outside window).
- All changes to prod require a release ticket and at least one reviewer from platform-sre.

Onboarding checklist for new infra engineer
1. Read this team wiki and related runbooks (links in Related Pages).
2. Get access to Vault and join infra Slack channels.
3. Complete sandbox apply training: run terraform apply against a tutorial module in the sandbox account.
4. Shadow oncall for two rotations.

Appendix: Template commands and snippets
- Assume role helper (bash):
  export AWS_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/InfraApplyRole
  aws sts assume-role --role-arn $AWS_ROLE_ARN --role-session-name infra-apply | jq -r .Credentials

- Quick plan check (CI local):
  terraform init -backend-config=backend.staging.tfvars
  terraform plan -var-file=override.tfvars -out=tfplan.binary

References and links
- Module registry: https://modules.internal.redwood.example.com
- Fleet dashboards: https://grafana.internal.redwood.example.com/d/fleet
- Runbooks folder: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks
